blocks.md: **Defender view.** Prevent: buy ECC memory for servers, apply firmware updates that raise refresh rates or improve in-DRAM mitigations, and do not expose cache-flush or uncached memory access to untrusted code where you control the sandbox (as NaCl did). Detect: ECC-equipped machines report corrected errors; a sudden rise on one host is worth investigating as either failing hardware or hammering. Respond: replace affected modules and treat a corrected-error storm on a multi-tenant host as a security event, not only a hardware ticket.

blocks.question: Why did the 2015 kernel exploit target page-table entries specifically?
options: One flipped bit in a PTE can redirect it to a page table the attacker controls, giving read-write access to all physical memory
Page tables are stored in the CPU cache, which is easier to hammer
PTEs are protected by ECC
The kernel rereads page tables every 64 ms
blocks.explain: A PTE holds a physical page number; flipping a low bit makes it point elsewhere. If it lands on one of the attacker's own page tables (memory was sprayed with them), the attacker can map any physical page.

blocks.question: A vendor says its DDR4 modules are 'Rowhammer-free because of TRR'. Which finding best tests that claim?
options: Kim et al. 2014 on DDR3
The Project Zero NaCl exploit
Cold boot attacks
TRRespass 2020, which flipped bits on 12 of 42 DDR4 modules by hammering many rows at once
blocks.explain: TRR tracks a limited number of aggressor rows. Many-sided hammering overwhelms the tracker, which TRRespass demonstrated on DDR4 modules sold with TRR.

lessons.title: Power, EM, sound and faults: physical side channels

blocks.md:
Plain idea: chips are built from transistors, and every time one switches, current flows. How much depends on *what* is being computed and on *which data*. An attacker who can measure the current, its radio emission or even the sound of the power circuitry watches the computation from the outside. And an attacker who can disturb the power or clock can make the chip compute *wrong* answers that reveal the key.

Paul Kocher, Joshua Jaffe and Benjamin Jun introduced two levels of power analysis in [Differential Power Analysis](https://www.paulkocher.com/doc/DifferentialPowerAnalysis.pdf) (CRYPTO 1999), with **smart cards** (bank, SIM and ID cards with a small processor) as the main target, since the attacker holds the card and can put a resistor in its power line.

**SPA** (simple power analysis) reads one trace directly. In their DES trace the 16 rounds are plainly visible, and conditional branches show up as different shapes. For RSA's square-and-multiply (lesson 2), squaring and multiplying often look different, so the trace spells out the operation sequence and the exponent bits with it. Their advice: avoid using secret values to choose branches; even then, some processors' microcode makes power depend on operand values.

blocks.title: Simple power analysis of square-and-multiply (toy exponent 1011)

scenes.caption: One power trace of the computation from lesson 2: seven operations. Squares (S) and multiplies (M) draw current differently, so they look different.
Reading it: an S followed by M is a 1 bit, an S alone is a 0 bit. S M, S, S M, S M gives 1, 0, 1, 1: the secret exponent, from a single trace.

Removing the visible pattern: perform the same operations for every bit (here S then M each time, discarding the unneeded result). SPA sees a uniform rhythm; data-dependent power remains for DPA, so add blinding too.

blocks.md: **DPA** (differential power analysis) works when single traces are too noisy. Record many traces with known inputs. Guess part of the key; for each trace, predict one bit of an intermediate value under that guess; split the traces into two groups by the predicted bit and subtract the group averages. With the right guess, the difference shows a spike where that bit is processed; with a wrong guess, the groups are random and the difference averages towards zero. Each key part is attacked separately, so the search is small. The authors reported a refined variant finding DES keys with fewer than 15 traces from most smart cards.

Their defences: reduce the signal (constant execution paths, balanced Hamming weights, shielding), add noise, and design protocols so leakage cannot accumulate (update keys often, limit how many times a key is used). They stress that signal reduction cannot reach zero against an attacker with unlimited samples.

**EM** analysis measures the same activity as radio emission, sometimes from a distance; the US government's classified TEMPEST programme, mentioned in the DPA paper, exists to contain such emanations.

**Defender view.** Prevent with evaluated hardware (smart cards and HSMs, hardware security modules, certified against physical attack) and physical control of devices; detect through tamper and glitch sensors where the chip logs them; respond by revoking keys held on lost or stolen devices.

**Sound, 2013.** Daniel Genkin, Adi Shamir and Eran Tromer extracted [full 4096-bit RSA keys](https://cs.tau.ac.il/~tromer/acoustic/) from GnuPG on several laptop models within an hour, from the sound of the voltage regulator's capacitors and coils during decryption of chosen ciphertexts, using a mobile phone next to the laptop or a parabolic microphone 4 metres away. Touching the laptop's chassis also worked as a probe. GnuPG fixed it (CVE-2013-4576) with countermeasures they proposed, and implementations using ciphertext blinding appeared less vulnerable.

**Hertzbleed, 2022.** Yingchen Wang and colleagues (University of Texas at Austin, UIUC and University of Washington) showed that **DVFS** (dynamic voltage and frequency scaling: the CPU lowers its clock to stay within power and thermal limits) makes the *frequency*, and so the running time, depend on power, and power depends on data. Power analysis became [remote timing](https://www.hertzbleed.com/): they extracted keys from SIKE (Supersingular Isogeny Key Encapsulation, a post-quantum candidate since broken by unrelated mathematics), implemented as "constant time", over the network. Frequency is measured in hertz (cycles per second), so frequency changes become time changes. CVE-2022-24436 (Intel) and CVE-2022-23823 (AMD); the researchers report that neither vendor planned microcode patches. Disabling Turbo Boost stops it in most cases, at a large performance cost.

**Fault injection.** Instead of watching, disturb: briefly drop the supply voltage (a **voltage glitch**), shorten a clock cycle, or pulse an EM field, so that one instruction computes a wrong result or is skipped. Dan Boneh, Richard DeMillo and Richard Lipton showed in 1997 that ["an implementation of RSA based on the Chinese Remainder Theorem can be broken using a single erroneous signature"](https://crypto.stanford.edu/~dabo/pubs/abstracts/faults.html): one half of the computation is wrong and the other right, and that mismatch reveals a prime factor of the key.

**Plundervolt (2019)**, from plunder (to steal something precious) and volt: Kit Murdock, David Oswald and Flavio Garcia (University of Birmingham) with Jo Van Bulck, Daniel Gruss and Frank Piessens used the software interface for undervolting Intel CPUs (normally a power-saving tweak) to inject faults into SGX enclaves, recovering keys and causing memory-safety errors. An attacker with root on the host is in SGX's threat model, so this mattered. Intel's fix: [microcode plus BIOS updates to disable the undervolting interface](https://plundervolt.com/), with the state visible in remote attestation.

The standard defence for signatures, which the 1997 paper's title asks for ("on the importance of checking"), is to verify a result before releasing it:

blocks.caption: Runnable. A toy RSA-CRT signer with a simulated fault and a check before release. Real implementations add hardware fault sensors too.

blocks.code:
normal : 588
glitch : fault detected: signature withheld
blocks.caption: Real output. 588 is the correct signature of 65. The glitched signature fails verification with the public key and is never released, so there is no faulty output to analyse.

blocks.md: Physical side channels need the attacker close to the device, but that is exactly the threat model of smart cards, phones, payment terminals, hardware wallets and secure enclaves. Hertzbleed shows the line between physical and remote is not fixed: when power controls frequency, power becomes timing.

blocks.question: In DPA, what tells the attacker that a key guess is right?
options: The card returns an error
Splitting the traces by a bit predicted under that guess gives group averages that differ clearly at some point in time, while wrong guesses give near-zero differences
A single trace shows the key bits directly
The power trace becomes shorter
blocks.explain: Correct guesses predict real intermediate values, so the split correlates with actual power use and the difference of means shows a spike. Wrong guesses split traces randomly.

blocks.question: Why did Hertzbleed affect code that was written to be constant-time?
options: CPU frequency scaling depends on power draw, which depends on data, so the same instructions run at different speeds for different data
The code had a secret-dependent branch
SIKE used lookup tables
The attack needed physical access to measure power
blocks.explain: Constant-time rules control which instructions and addresses run. Hertzbleed changes how fast the same instructions run, through data-dependent power and frequency, and needs no power probe.

lessons.title: Trusted hardware: TPMs, measured boot and secure enclaves

blocks.md:
Plain idea: if the operating system can be compromised, keys should live somewhere it cannot reach, and the machine should be able to *prove* what software it booted. Trusted hardware is a small, separate component with its own protected storage and a narrow interface.

Why keys in normal RAM are not enough: J. Alex Halderman and colleagues at Princeton showed in 2008 with **cold boot attacks** that DRAM contents [fade over seconds to minutes](https://freedom-to-tinker.com/2008/02/21/new-research-result-cold-boot-attacks-disk-encryption/) after power is cut, and far longer when chilled (around minus 50 degrees Celsius with an inverted can of compressed air, the chips kept data for ten minutes or more out of the machine). They read disk-encryption keys out of memory and defeated BitLocker (Windows' disk encryption) despite its TPM (Trusted Platform Module, explained next), because the TPM had already released the key into RAM.

**TPM** (Trusted Platform Module), specified by the Trusted Computing Group (TCG), is either a discrete chip or a hardware-protected mode of the main processor. Per Microsoft's [TPM documentation](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/security/hardware-security/tpm/switch-pcr-banks-on-tpm-2-0-devices) and related pages, it provides:

- Keys whose private part never leaves the TPM, including the **endorsement key**, an RSA key pair held inside it.
- **PCRs** (Platform Configuration Registers): registers that cannot be written, only *extended*. Each new value is the hash of the old value concatenated with the new measurement. A PC TPM has at least 24 PCRs, and the first 16 reset only when the TPM itself resets.
- **Sealing**: a key can be bound to expected PCR values and is released only if they match, which is how BitLocker ties the disk key to an untampered boot.
- **Anti-hammering**: after too many wrong PINs, the TPM locks out further guesses for a while.

blocks.caption: The extend operation. Order matters and no step can be undone, so the final value commits to the whole boot sequence.

scenes.caption: Firmware measures the bootloader (hashes it) and extends a PCR with that hash before running it. Secure Boot (os-security-isolation course) checks signatures; measured boot records what ran.
Each stage measures the next before handing over, and also appends an entry to an event log kept in normal memory.
Attestation: a verifier sends a fresh random nonce; the TPM signs the PCR values plus the nonce with a key only it holds.
The verifier replays the event log, recomputes the expected PCRs and compares. A match proves the log is genuine; the log shows what booted.
Unsealing: the OS asks for the disk key. The TPM releases it only because the PCRs equal the values it was sealed to. A modified bootloader would change the PCRs and the key would stay sealed.

blocks.code:
import hashlib

def extend(pcr, component):
    measurement = hashlib.sha256(component).digest()
    return hashlib.sha256(pcr + measurement).digest()   # PCR = H(PCR || new)

def boot(chain):
    pcr = bytes(32)                     # PCRs start at zero after reset
    for component in chain:
        pcr = extend(pcr, component)
    return pcr.hex()[:16]

good = [b"firmware v1.2", b"bootloader v7", b"kernel 6.12"]
evil = [b"firmware v1.2", b"bootloader v7 + bootkit", b"kernel 6.12"]
swap = [b"bootloader v7", b"firmware v1.2", b"kernel 6.12"]

print("expected boot :", boot(good))
print("tampered boot :", boot(evil))
print("same parts, other order:", boot(swap))
blocks.caption: Runnable model of PCR extension with SHA-256. Shows the first 16 hex digits of the final PCR.

blocks.code:
expected boot : 889ba8a4c8997388
tampered boot : 3a5d19c89cee5be1
same parts, other order: 1d63841adffe148e
blocks.caption: Real output. Changing one component, or only the order, gives an unrelated final value, so a key sealed to the expected value will not unseal.

blocks.md:
Cold boot still matters: the TPM protects the key until boot, then the OS must hold it in RAM to use it. Microsoft's [BitLocker countermeasures](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/security/operating-system-security/data-protection/bitlocker/countermeasures) recommend **preboot authentication** (a PIN before the key is ever loaded) against memory remanence and DMA (direct memory access, a device reading RAM without the CPU) attacks, and use the TCG's Memory Overwrite Request to clear RAM on reset. And the TPM is only as good as its own code: lesson 15's ROCA case broke RSA keys generated inside Infineon TPMs.

**Secure enclaves** go further: run code in isolation from the OS on the main processor.

- **Intel SGX** (Software Guard eXtensions): an application creates an **enclave**, a private memory region in the **EPC** (Enclave Page Cache) that only code inside it can access; per the [Linux kernel's SGX documentation](https://docs.kernel.org/arch/x86/sgx.html) it is encrypted before it leaves the last-level cache. Intel has since deprecated SGX on client Core processors (from the 11th and 12th generations) and keeps it on Xeon servers; cloud confidential computing has moved to whole-VM TEEs such as [Intel TDX](https://docs.kernel.org/arch/x86/tdx.html) and AMD SEV-SNP. The threat model includes a malicious OS, which made SGX the favourite target of this course's attacks: Foreshadow extracted attestation keys, Plundervolt faulted enclaves by undervolting, and the 2022 SGX.Fail study showed real deployments (the Secret Network blockchain, CyberLink PowerDVD) could not keep up with SGX's patch cycle.

- **Arm TrustZone** splits the processor into a **secure world** and a **non-secure world**, separated in hardware; software called the **secure monitor** switches between them. The secure world typically runs a trusted OS forming a **TEE** (Trusted Execution Environment) for authentication, payment keys and DRM, per [Arm's overview](https://www.arm.com/technologies/trustzone-for-cortex-a).
- **Apple's Secure Enclave** is a separate subsystem on the chip, isolated from the main processor, with its own Boot ROM, AES engine and protected memory, running sepOS on an L4 microkernel. Per [Apple's Platform Security guide](https://support.apple.com/guide/security/secure-enclave-sec59b0b31ff/web), it runs at a lower clock speed partly to resist clock and power attacks; its Memory Protection Engine encrypts and authenticates its memory with anti-replay protection (A11 and later); and a per-device UID key is fused into the chip at manufacture; from the A9 on it is generated inside the Secure Enclave so that it is not available to Apple or its suppliers.

The trend is from *sharing a core* (SGX: enclave and attacker on the same core, so every lesson 5 to 11 channel applies) towards *separate processors* (Secure Enclave, discrete TPMs), which removes most shared microarchitectural state.

An enclave or TEE protects against software that cannot reach its memory. It does not remove side channels: if enclave code runs on the same core as the attacker, its cache footprint, branch history and timing are as observable as any other program's. Enclave code must still be constant-time.

blocks.question: BitLocker seals the disk key to PCR values. An attacker replaces the bootloader with one that logs keystrokes. What happens at the next boot?
options: The TPM detects the new bootloader's signature and deletes the key
Nothing: PCRs only record the kernel
The bootloader's hash changes the PCR value, so the TPM refuses to unseal the key and recovery is needed
The attacker's bootloader can reset the PCR to the old value
blocks.explain: Extend is one-way and order-sensitive, and the first 16 PCRs reset only with the TPM. A different bootloader produces different PCRs, so the sealed key stays locked.

blocks.question: Why were SGX enclaves hit by so many of the attacks in this course, while Apple's Secure Enclave largely avoids that class?
options: SGX does not encrypt memory
SGX enclaves run on the same cores as untrusted code and share caches, buffers and predictors; the Secure Enclave is a separate processor
Apple's enclave has no cache
SGX only runs in the cloud
blocks.explain: Transient execution and cache attacks need shared microarchitectural state. A separate processor with its own memory protection has far less of it, though physical attacks remain.

lessons.title: Hardware supply chain, coordinated disclosure, and practice

blocks.md: Plain idea: with software you can read, patch and redeploy. With hardware you inherit silicon, ROM and firmware that you cannot inspect and sometimes cannot change, from vendors several steps up the supply chain. Four real cases show the shapes this takes:

- **Unpatchable ROM.** checkm8 (2019) is a use-after-free in the SecureROM boot code of Apple's A5 to A11 chips (iPhone 4S to iPhone X). CERT/CC's (the CERT Coordination Center, which publishes vulnerability notes) [note](https://www.kb.cert.org/vuls/id/941987) explains that because SecureROM is read-only, it cannot be patched by a firmware update; exploitation needs physical access and DFU (Device Firmware Update) mode, and does not persist across reboots.
- **Unupdatable memory.** Phoenix's authors note that DRAM in the field cannot be updated (lesson 12).

- **Certified but flawed.** ROCA (2017; from its paper's title, The Return of Coppersmith's Attack, a factoring method it extends): an RSA key-generation library from Infineon, in devices certified to FIPS 140-2 (the US standard for cryptographic modules) and Common Criteria EAL 5+ (a high Evaluation Assurance Level), produced primes with a [structure that allowed factoring](https://acmccs.github.io/papers/p1631-nemecA.pdf) 1024- and 2048-bit keys. It shipped in TPMs, ID cards, passports and tokens since at least 2012; the authors estimated tens of millions of affected devices. Keys had to be regenerated, not patched.
- **Undocumented hardware.** In Operation Triangulation (2023), an iPhone attack chain wrote to [hardware registers unused by Apple's firmware](https://securelist.com/operation-triangulation-the-last-hardware-mystery/111669/) to bypass the Page Protection Layer (CVE-2023-38606). Researchers at Kaspersky, the security company that found the attack, guessed it was a debug or test feature.

Add firmware that runs with more privilege than the OS, like Intel AMT in lesson 3 or the UEFI firmware that starts every PC, and the defender's job becomes:

- **Inventory**: which CPU models, microcode, firmware, TPM and DRAM you run, by machine.
- **Update channels**: prefer platforms whose firmware and microcode you can actually update, and track vendor advisories.
- **Attestation**: measured boot and TPM quotes (lesson 14) to notice firmware you did not expect.
- **Key hygiene**: when a chip's key generation or isolation fails, rotate keys it produced or protected; the ROCA researchers published a tool to test public keys for the flaw.

**Coordinated disclosure for hardware.** A software bug usually has one vendor; a CPU bug needs the chip vendor, microcode, every OS, every hypervisor, browsers and cloud providers ready on one day. The Spectre and Meltdown timeline:

1. 1 June 2017: Jann Horn reports variants 1 and 2 to Intel, AMD and Arm; variant 3 (Meltdown) follows. Other teams report independently, and the papers' authors join a shared embargo.
2. Late 2017: Linux developers merge KPTI in public. The Register noted on 2 January 2018 that comments in the patches had been redacted while an embargo was due to lift.
3. 3 January 2018: Google publishes ahead of the [originally coordinated date of 9 January](https://security.googleblog.com/2018/01/todays-cpu-vulnerability-what-you-need.html) "because of existing public reports and growing speculation in the press and security research community".
4. Afterwards: Spectre v2 mitigations were still being written in public; LWN called the situation "chaotic".

blocks.title: Spectre and Meltdown: from report to disclosure

scenes.caption: 1 June 2017: Project Zero reports variants 1 and 2 to Intel, AMD and Arm. Meltdown follows later; other academic teams report the same issues independently.
Vendors bring OS developers and cloud providers under embargo. Fixes need microcode, kernels, hypervisors and compilers to change together.
Kernel page-table isolation lands in public Linux trees with redacted comments. Observers notice an unusual rush.
3 January 2018: with details leaking, Google and the researchers publish six days early. Patches for Meltdown are ready; Spectre fixes keep arriving for months.

blocks.md: Since then the Linux kernel has a written process for [embargoed hardware issues](https://docs.kernel.org/process/embargoed-hardware-issues.html): a separate hardware security team reachable on an encrypted mailing list, a Memorandum of Understanding instead of NDAs, mitigations published to everyone at the same moment when the embargo ends, and a request that embargoes be "constrained to the minimum time" needed, not stretched "to meet conference talk dates or other non-technical reasons". Embargo lengths still vary a lot:

]
for name, reported, public in cases:

blocks.md:
**Practice, legally.** Everything in this course must be tried only on machines you own or are explicitly authorised to test; laws such as the US CFAA and the UK Computer Misuse Act (security-basics) apply to hardware attacks too.

- [pwn.college Microarchitecture Exploitation](https://pwn.college/system-security/speculative-execution/) (Arizona State University's free platform): lectures and challenges on Flush+Reload, Meltdown and Spectre in provided environments.
- [ChipWhisperer](https://github.com/newaetech/chipwhisperer) by NewAE: an open-source toolchain and tutorials for power analysis and glitching on your own target boards.
- On your own machine: rerun this course's comparison timing and simulator code, read your `/sys/devices/system/cpu/vulnerabilities` files, and check crypto code you maintain against the three constant-time rules.

Hardware security in one sentence: the hardware runs your program correctly, but not invisibly. Keep secrets out of shared state (constant-time code, isolation, separate secure processors), keep firmware and microcode current, measure what booted, and expect new variants.

blocks.question: Why can checkm8 never be fixed on affected devices, unlike a bug in iOS?
options: Apple chose not to patch it
It needs a network connection that cannot be blocked
The exploit is persistent across reboots
It lives in SecureROM, read-only boot code inside the chip, which firmware updates cannot change
blocks.explain: CERT/CC: SecureROM is read-only, so it cannot be patched. The mitigating factors are physical access, DFU mode, and that the exploit does not persist across reboots.

blocks.question: The Linux kernel's hardware embargo process asks for embargoes to be as short as possible. Which reason does its documentation give?
options: Long embargoes force developers to keep private patches up to date with ongoing kernel development, creating extra work and conflicts
Shorter embargoes make CVEs cheaper
Hardware vendors prefer short embargoes
Researchers cannot publish papers during an embargo
blocks.explain: The document says extending embargoes for non-technical reasons such as conference dates creates more work and burden, because patches must keep tracking upstream changes.

blocks.question: Your company's code-signing tokens are found to contain an Infineon chip affected by ROCA. What is the necessary response?
options: Apply a firmware update; existing keys are then safe
Generate new keys on unaffected hardware and revoke the old public keys, because the existing keys can be factored from the public key alone
Nothing, because the tokens are FIPS 140-2 certified
Increase the RSA key length in the existing certificates
blocks.explain: ROCA's flaw is in how the primes were generated. Anyone with the public key can attempt the factorisation, so the keys themselves are weak: regenerate and revoke. Certification did not catch it. For long-lived signing keys, also plan the move to post-quantum signatures: NIST IR 8547 deprecates RSA after 2030.
